utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Bourgon I don't see, and Mr. Haynes. Good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you to enjoy the weekend and the weather, but there wasn't much to enjoy. So you're back. We'll try and do our utmost to finish with your testimony as soon as possible. I appreciate your patience having been here for over two weeks already. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Last Wednesday now, my learned colleague, Madam Fauveau, showed you a document authored by President Karadzic wherein he seemed to be trying to assert some control over the VRS, and you characterized it as an exclusively political document and said that you thought that those in power at that time feared a military coup or something to that effect; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you a letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 3928.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- that you wrote to President Karadzic in May of 1995, and we'll just wait for it to come up. And I want to give you an opportunity to review it. There is a cover page transmitting it to the president from General Mladic. I think basically he put a cover letter on your letter and then transmitted the letter. Do you see that, sir? Sorry, we just need an audible yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I received the letter in person that in accordance with the military rules, I forwarded to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move to the second page of this document so you can see the letter that you wrote to President Karadzic. And just take your time, and let us know when you've had a chance to read it and refresh your recollection about it. Are we ready to go down to the bottom of the page, General, if there is some more?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little smudged here, so there is one sentence that is completely illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a cleaner copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Unfortunately we don't, Mr. President, this is as good as we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Otherwise we're -- it's not clear, we could zoom in there. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Alternatively, I could read the English translation and see if that helps the General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as item 3 in is concerned, well, the second part, the sense of the sentence seems to get lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, well, what I can do, General, is I can read you the English translation. We seem to have a -- a translation that was legible. Paragraph 3 states: "In all the armies in the world, the appropriate means of official communication of the Supreme Commander are decrees, written and verbal orders, congratulatory notes, et cetera, but not letters. Because of this, we do not know how to understand the evaluations and positions presented in the letter -- or in a letter. Are they intended for discussion rather than implementation, or are we to understand them as duties and orders?"

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've understood now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I see paragraph 4 is a little illegible, so I will the just go ahead and read the first couple of sentences of that paragraph for you: "This war we are waging has entered a new and decisive stage. Although the some total of your combat achievements is still very high, there are some extremely negative developments and trends which increasingly undermine our superiority in weapons. In a situation like this, we must seek new solutions for the most important problems in the further conduct of the war because the methods used so far can no longer produce such good combat results." And I'll just leave the document where it is, so you can scan the rest of the letter and freshen your recollection. And just let us know whenever you think you are ready to answer some questions about it, if you think it's jogged your memory enough. If you need to read the whole letter, please let us know and we'll give you as much time as you need, General.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the second page, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. We may have the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read through the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall writing this letter, General, and the general events which prompted you to write the letter?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To put it briefly, this letter, in response to President Karadzic's letter, came on the heels of the Sanski Most assembly meeting in April of 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, apparently President Karadzic wrote his letter accusing the army and the Main Staff of plotting a military coup or a putsch of some kind, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to explain this somewhat. The main reason for Mr. Karadzic drafting his letter was that the generals weren't happy about the decision of the president after the Assembly in Sanski Most, the decision to replace General Mladic. And they wouldn't replace him with anyone else. They would have some coordinator for the army of the Serbian Krajina and the Republika Srpska army. The generals met in Banja Luka two days later and adopted a conclusion, according to which, at that point in time, when the vital interests of the Serbs were a threat, this was an unproductive act, a senseless act, the result of which would be to weaken the ranks of the army. And the consequences could be serious, because to replace the commander at that point in time when the end of the war was in sight, was not a good idea. The decision that we signed and forwarded to him as the Supreme Commander was taken by the president to mean that a military putsch was being prepared, and he then sent a letter to all of us who had signed the document. I was prepared to be replaced at that point in time, Your Honours, because in life there are times when you have to be held accountable for your position. So regardless of how serious the consequences might be, I believe that I acted correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at paragraph 5 of the letter, you say that - and this is regarding President Karadzic's letter - quote: "Your letter is also inspired by the mistrust of the officers of the army of Republika Srpska nurtured by some representatives of the civilian authorities since the very beginning of the war." And is that the same mistrust that we spoke about the other day, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one way in which there was a lack of trust, but this letter was written because of those events. As for that lack of trust, well, all I can say, is that something that has to do with the beginning of the war. I'll provide you with one example. Sometime in September 1993 there was a revolt of a certain number of soldiers in Banja Luka. They revolted because some population had been placed under a burden because of corruption, looting, and so on. This was positive, but later on they went to the other extreme. They took over the Assembly building and they, in fact, tried to seize power. In an interview on television one day later, Mr. Karadzic, President Karadzic, told the journalists that the situation would calm down. He said that these were justified demands made by the soldiers and by some officers, and when asked whether this could happen in other towns, such as Bijeljina, he categorically stated that was impossible in Bijeljina. He said he had a good commander there, Ljubisa Savic Mauzer, and he would not allow this to happen. Ljubisa Savic Mauzer was a commander of a light brigade, 800 men strong. It was under my command. I had 30.000 men under my command, but he believed that Ljubisa would present this. Not the corps commander. We who weren't in the party, obviously, weren't quite trusted by our president or by other government representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we'll talk about Mauzer and his panthers in a little while, General. I want to turn your attention to paragraph 6 of the letter, and again I'll just quote it or you can look at it there. It should be in front of you. You say: "Further to your order to prevent anything that is against the constitution or the law, we assure you that this command shall continue to operate in the spirit of law and thoroughly analyse the quality of people employed in organs for morale, religious and legal affairs, and organs for security and intelligence."

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already said that in the course of the war, these organs were under a lot of pressure for them to become politically engaged; or, rather, they wanted to have people joining them who followed the party line, people from the SDS party, because it was obvious that they were a thorn in the side of the local and central authorities because they did not deal certain political problems at a local level by having recourse to military means.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And on Friday you referred to the efforts to replace General Gvero and, if you recall, at the Sanski Most Assembly meeting there were also calls to replace General Tolimir. I take it that that's what that paragraph you just read refers to?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I've -- you told us on Friday that General Mladic refused to dismiss General Gvero; and you, yourself, weren't sure whether part of his reason for doing that was solidarity with General Gvero or General Mladic's - in your words - intolerance and dislike of the Supreme Commander; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I'm not sure what took precedence, but it's quite obvious that both these factors played a role.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the antipathy between President Karadzic and General Mladic was mutual, was it not?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case. It had its ups and downs in the course of the war. Sometimes they were a little closer and sometimes not so close to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you another exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- and this is 3931.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Take a moment and review the document if you would, General, it was shown to you, I believe, during a 2007 interview with the OTP. Do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours. I'll tell you what the purpose of the document is. Before retiring, the superior officer has to have a discussion and has to examine all the document that concern the person who is retiring. I did not have the possibility -- well, let me say this first: General Mladic at the time was placed at the disposal of the Main Staff. He maintained a certain status quo, he didn't come to work, we didn't see him, but his position in service hasn't been changed; and the president of the Republika Srpska is responsible for his position, not the chief of the Main Staff. When the president of the republic issued a decision on retiring, General Mladic, a personnel staff member told me of an error. He had an assessment at the highest level of one's official assessment, and as a result of this assessment you have certain benefits. If you have such a grade after one-year's service, you have one salary level extra. So this means you have a higher salary. This wasn't done in good time and in a certain manner, we tried to correct the error. The assessment of General Mladic was made by President Karadzic or the Ministry of Defence because they are responsible for it. I, as the chief of the Main Staff wasn't responsible for this matter. So as a result of this, his treatment was more favourable, at least as far as the pension he was to receive is concerned. So this is a quite regular procedure that is followed whenever a member of the military retires.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just scroll down on the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Then we see your signature there, correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to an assessment, is that assessment another way of saying job performance appraisal? Was it an evaluation of the quality of General Mladic's work, is that what you were referring to, General, that was conducted by President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I take it that's because there was nobody higher other than the Supreme Commander or the president during peacetime to do that, yourself or had it been General Milovanovic wouldn't be in a position to evaluate his commander, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there is a box: "Conclusion of the latest performance appraisal and date of appraisal." It's the second box we see, and to the right of that it says: "Excellent -- 4.88, 10 January 1995." Can you explain what that means, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that that was the last time his performance was evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what does "4.88" mean? Is that a score out of a possibility of some other score?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The score is between 1 and 5. This is almost 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when this application by General Mladic through his assistant came in 2002, he had been under indictment by this Tribunal for several years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but he was not relieved of his duties. He was still a professional officer. He hadn't retired. He was at the disposal of the authorities before a decision was taken what would happen to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move on to 65 ter 3938, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's another assessment I'll be showing you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could not have this particular document broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My understanding for the record is that pursuant to the agreement entered into between the party that furnished the document, it is to remain in private session under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see what's on your screen before you?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an evaluation for Major General Gvero, Milan, from 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And would you take your time and please read this document, and continue through it as a -- as you need.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time, and could I be shown the other pages as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, General. If you are ready to move, we will turn the page.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've reviewed the first page, can I have the second, please. I can't see the descriptive part. The bottom part of the page, please. That's fine, thank you. I've read the document through, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, you correctly noted that the first page of the document indicates that this the assessment was dated 1992. Having read the text of the document which refers to events subsequent to 1992 and, if you look at the dates of the signatures being October 1995, October 30th of 1995, when General Mladic signed off on the assessment; and November 5th, 1995 for when General Gvero put his signature on the assessment, can we agree that this particular text here, this final conclusion was done in 1995 for this period indicated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer the question, wait, please, General. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to the method of examination regarding the date, because the Prosecutor omitted to mention the period to which the assessment applies, and that is the 31st of August 1988, until the 31st of August 1992, which I think is of the greatest importance and that is stated on the 1st page of this document. So the assessment applies to this period. This is a period that is not covered by the indictment, though the actual assessment was given in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just going to draw your attention to this detail. Obviously, in the Main Staff they were late in the regular assessment of their officers. Somebody failed to do their duty, and, probably, because of their salaries and promotions they were cautioned that they had to do these assessments because it is normal to make assessments every two or three years. So probably in 1995 there were two assessments, for the period up to 1992 and another one for the period up to 1995. So the person who wrote this assessment made certain errors, because in the assessment for 1992 he could not have mention the participation in Operation Lukavac in 1993. I'm not saying it's incorrectly written, but there are errors. He cannot be appraised for this particular activity when it came in the following period. Now, whether the error was made in the actual writing or in the typing out, but obviously this is an assessment for the period up to 1992 even though it was signed in 1995. There probably was another assessment, an official assessment, for the period up to 1995; and I don't know whether the gentleman do have that document at their disposal. I don't know what the official conclusion and assessment for the following period is. As for this first period, General Gvero was assessed with a 5.0, that is the maximum score that can be given to an officer, exemplary in every sense of the word. And this assessment implies certain things, General Gvero could have a year later in 1993, have moved up on the salary scale; and he could have already been promoted to the next rank, lieutenant-colonel general. So I'm talking according to the rules of service, to indicate that such a high assessment carries certain privileges and benefits for the person involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that cover your question, or do you wish to add something to it, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do have just one or two follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Before you proceed, General, as far as you can tell us, there was only one Lukavac 1993. Was there any other Lukavac, say, 1992, 1991, was there anything like that, or only 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only 1993, Your Honours. There were no other similar operations earlier on. So that's why I'm saying that the text is incorrect. It may have been copied from the next one, but this is just a hypothesis. I don't know. I haven't seen the other document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And General, again, that's why I put the question the way I did to you. Because clearly this assessment involves or is assessing General Gvero's performance after August of 1992. As we all know the series of battles for the Podrinje in the Drina river valley, the whole Cerska campaign that ultimately led to the creation of the safe area of Srebrenica, that all went into 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this line of questioning. No mention of Cerska or campaign in the Drina river valley mentioned, only the operation of Podrinje, which is a far broader concept than the Drina river valley, and it could mean something else. So when referring to the document, I think it is not correct to say things that are not mentioned in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't agree with the kind of approach you are taking to this document, Mr. Krgovic. Let the witness answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Podrinje is the entire territory along the Drina river valley, and operations were conducted from Gorazde as far as Zvornik and including Zvornik. So, of course, it is your right not to agree with Mr. Krgovic, but I personally think that in this context he is right; but I did understand the Prosecutor. There were certain operations in 1993, too, but this assessment is for 1992 inclusive and not 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the paramilitaries a little bit more, General. In your corps' area of responsibility, there was a paramilitary leader with the nickname of Mando. His real name was Mitar Maksimovic. Do you recall him, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he was a self-styled captain, one of these fellows that gave himself a rank, but he became formally part of the 1st Majevica Brigade in Ugljevik eventually; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was an order of the Main Staff saying that all paramilitary forces have to be part of the army of Republika Srpska and put under its command or, alternatively, to be disarmed. When I was arrived at the corps, there were several such forces, there was the Lajnovic Brigade at Majevica, there was Crni Lugar in Samac, and around Brcko as well, there were such elements who were not under the control of the army. With all our available forces and with the support of all professional officers, we managed to disarm those who refused to be placed under our command and to transform -- transport them across the border and hand them over to the security forces of Serbia. And in most cases these were criminals who had already problems with the law. Mando's unit varied between 4 to 1 battalion, but compared with the others, he did place himself under the command of the command of the 1st Majevica Brigade. I can't speak about his activities before he was placed under our command, nor do I wish to have any responsibilities in that regard, but after he placed himself under our command, he acted fairly and professionally even though he was not a professional soldier. And I must say, that all those paramilitary elements were in a certain sense party-oriented. I must say that at the beginning, I had problems with the Bijeljina Panthers; and I had to add to them a number of professional officers in order to be able to control them. But, at times, they would learn about their deployment before I did. That was the case with respect to a Bratunac and some other operations. And I saw that they were preparing themselves, and I asked, What you are you doing? And they would say, Well, you will get the order soon, and then subsequently I would get an order from President Karadzic that they were to act outside the corps zone, which was a surprise to me. Obviously, there were certain lines that I did not belong to and I was the last to learn about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, why don't we talk about the Panthers now for a couple of moments. When you refer to the Bratunac operation. Correct me if I'm wrong, I believe your referring to an operation in early 1993 when the Panteri were sent to the area of Bratunac in response to some armija or ABiH attacks in that area, specifically the attack on the village of Kravica in January of 1993. Is that what you're referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I later learned that Bratunac itself was in jeopardy because of the activities of these units from the Srebrenica enclave, and that is why they sought the assistance of the unit, and they did go there; and upon the completion of the task, they returned to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mauzer's real name was Ljubisa Savic, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours. He was not the brigade commander throughout the war. I think at the end of 1994 -- at the end of 1994, he started to show certain political ambitions, and I told him, if he wished to go into politics he had to hand over his military duties. And he agreed, and Ljubisa Lazic was appointed to his position and who successfully led the unit until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, he was a self-styled major but in actuality had no professional military qualifications that you're aware of; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. And General Mladic personally ordered him to remove the rank at the meeting of the 2nd of September 1992 in Bijeljina. And he received his first officer's rank of 2nd lieutenant, then he was lieutenant, and finally captain. So he never reached the rank of major, maybe towards the end of the war; but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you ever hear, General, that in 1992 he and his unit at that time were thought to be involved in the murder of Muslims in the Bijeljina area?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I arrived in Bijeljina, I heard all kinds of stories from various sources. But I didn't have the real information. I learned about this in 2004 when I was interviewed by your colleagues from the OTP; and they told me that there was a whole file of indictments, accusations and charges against Mauzer for events that occurred before I arrived in Bijeljina. At the time I didn't have that knowledge. Whether this was concealed from me, maybe I wasn't the suitable person for this, in any event I was not aware of those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mauzer's Panthers were also referred sometimes as the special brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, until they were reformed to form the Bijeljina Light Infantry Brigade. That was the official name, but they continued to call themselves the Panthers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So just before we move on to another topic, so both Mando and Mauzer eventually became absorbed into your corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I understand what you've told us that with respect to Mauzer's unit, your experience was that President Karadzic had his own line of communication with them on occasion, but in other respects they were treated as any other element of your corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. I did not wish to receive direct orders from anyone except from General Mladic, so that they came to see me too; but they obviously had a more direct line of communication that I was not part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, on to another topic, General. You told us last Thursday that you studied the Geneva Conventions together with the foot soldiers as well as the officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the very beginning of the war, from the Minister of Defence, General Subotic, we received instructions and the integral text of the Geneva Conventions, and a special section on treatment of prisoners. We copied this and we handed it out to each soldier, and we took some other measures; for instance, we didn't have those plates for identity markings, but we ordered a card to be filled in with basic information that every soldier must carry in the left-top pocket, just as he had to carry the first-aid bandage in his lower pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in your 2004 interview with the OTP, you specifically stated that in 1989, when you were serving in the 329 Armoured Brigade, that you recall receiving the 1998 JNA Regulations on the Application of International Laws of War in the Armed Forces of the SFRY. Can you confirm that, sir, that you recall receiving that document?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. Those documents in the training process of soldiers and officers were all regularly studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think you told us that you actually planned the brigade-wide training in accordance those regulations; is that correct, sir? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And they were transmitted down to the battalion level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, training was done at the level of the company and platoons, so it was passed on to the level of every individual soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us about the Batkovic prison camp and that when you arrived to assume your duties as corps commander, you didn't like what you saw and heard about it, so you commissioned a report to be done; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I took over my duties I ordered and formed a commission to establish the real state of affairs in the Batkovic camp because I heard some contradictory reports upon my arrival. I personally never entered the camp. The commission was composed of Lieutenant-Colonel Mitrovic, who is a Professor, who is still working at the fault in Bijeljina; a sociology professor; a physician; somebody from the security organ; and I think one person from the logistics department, to make an assessment of the logistics support there. And the report I received from them the next day was alarming and unbelievable for me, because there were persons in the camp who could not be under any circumstances be considered prisoners of war. There were 80 persons, civilians, among them a few were under age. They were simply picked up from their homes in Zvornik and Kozluk and brought there. Apart from that, the commission found that the security was inadequate and composed of reservists from the surrounding villages who were abusing the closeness of their homes and acting in a non-military fashion; so that I ordered that the command of the camp be arrested, that the guards be suspended and sent to the front lines, and that military policemen be deployed who have the necessary training for that purpose to guard the camp. Unfortunately I found that a those policemen too, later on, informed the commander what was in store for him and he fled to Serbia. And then I had to dismiss the entire battalion and form a completely new one because I could not trust them to perform properly their military police role. So, as you see, I had to do some really big spring cleaning when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked during your 2004 OTP interview, General, whether you sent that report up to the Main Staff, and you answered that you did report to them, and I'll just quote what you said: "It was incorporated into the morale report, and it was sent to General Gvero, while the security chief reported to Tolimir." And I just want to clarify, if we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page please, page.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Page 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify that answer, if we could, because on Friday, I believe you testified that all reports went out under your name, under your signature, to your commander. So when you said in your interview that the report was sent to General Gvero, I take it you mean that it was forwarded to him by Mladic or somebody at the Main Staff since it's obviously relevant to General Gvero's professional expertise, is that what -- is that what happened, sir?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need to clarify something here for better understanding. I cannot directly respond. The report was sent to the Main Staff. General Mladic received it when the mail was sorted. We would send -- forward those documents we felt needed to be sent there. The report was sent to General Gvero, because I felt that it would cause a certain political problem because those people ended up in the camp because of the politics. Had there been good will to release them, they had three months time to do it. They didn't have to wait for me. And I knew that once I released them, I would be exposed to major pressure from the local and probably also the central political authorities, this is why I forwarded it. In the report I said that I had established a permanent commission including personnel from the morale section. There was one man from there who was responsible for monitoring, and I felt that he would be the best person to do that. This was from the morale section. I didn't know how the Main Staff would make up such a commission, but I felt that these people were professional, and they would do the job properly. That man was in charge of humanitarian cooperation at my section, so was communicating with the UNHCR and UNPROFOR. He also attended some meetings of the civilian authorities where these relations were discussed. So for this reason, I sent it to General Gvero, by the nature of their work, the security organs monitor the security aspects of the camp via the military police; and that is why I wanted them to inform the Main Staff along their line of reporting that we had relieved the old one and were going to form a new police battalion. This is a pretty drastic measure, and it creates a kind of vacuum which can be dangerous if it remains unresolved. The military police also provide security for me, for the command, and also carries out military security police in the field and provides services for the military prosecuting organs, which are not under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt, could we just be clear that this is 1992. That's clear from the context of the page 188.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, do you agree to that, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly. It's been clear, I think, from his testimony, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just to follow-up on the last thing you mentioned, General, and with respect to Batkovic, it was your MPs, your corps MPs, up through 1995 who were responsible for securing that facility guarding whatever prisoners were there from 1992 to 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked in your 2004 interview about reporting on morale to your superior command. And I just want to read to you some portions of the interview. We don't have a B/C/S -- we don't have a transcript in your language, General. And I want to make sure that I'm capturing this portion correctly so you understand the full context of this part of the interview. You're asked by the investigator, a man named Paul Grady, he says and this is at page 172: "We have a lot of reports from Gvero. So does Gvero write a morale report, send it to the corps, you give it to Jelacic and say, 'Give this out to my brigade commanders.'" And you responded: "Let's not confuse command levels. I report to the Main Staff. The Main Staff does not report to me. They issue orders to me, just like brigade commanders report to me, but I order them. When Jelacic received all the reports from the brigades with both positive and negative influences, examples of morale influences, which both had to be included in the report, Gvero would receive that report just like the reports he would receive from other units. They would then assess morale on the whole, in the army, based on these reports." You were asked a follow-up question, let me -- the investigator wants to give you a couple of examples, and then he shows you an example. You look at it, and you say the following: "They would be sent on a monthly basis, and only there would be extraordinary exceptional reports only if there were really, really serious problems. First there would be the first elements, area to be reported on was positive influences on morale. So first you had to look at this from a positive angle. The second item was the positive example of individuals and units. Then the next one was negative influences on morale, then exceptionally negative events that happened, and then there was the assessment. So you weigh out both the good and the bad and then measures to be taken by our command in order to improve the situation." Let me just stop right there. I've spoken for a while. And this is still in the middle of your answer, so I want to let you process now and then I will ask you about the rest of your answer. In your experience as the corps commander, General, is that how these monthly reports were written in your corps and then transmitted up to the Main Staff? Is that essentially how it worked, or is there anything you would like to add or subtract from what I've just read to you from your statement?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, just like all the other combat readiness elements, I am responsible for morale as commander. My professional organs writes, makes the assessments and so on, and comes out at the meeting with their assessment, and then if we agree with it then the document is drafted. The document is written, goes to the Main Staff with my signature at the bottom, and then is forwarded on to General Mladic, General Gvero, and they also look at those items that are of interest to them. So based on all the compiled reports, they meet, assess morale, in the whole of the army and propose measures. We need to separate certain things here, or differentiate between certain things. There are proposals, what can be done at any level or at all levels, to improve morale. There are things that can be done at the brigade level. The brigade can do it on its own, but they need to be directed to do that. Where this is not possible, we send somebody from my staff to help them in this or somebody from the professional organ, or some of my other assistants. There are also things that can be done at the level of the corps. And in our assessment there are also things that the main -- the Supreme Command should do which would be essential to be dealt with and which have an adverse influence on overall morale on the army. This is just the usual way to gather data on the morale in the units on assessing it and proposals to the command organs what needs to be done to improve it; but the ultimate decision rests with the commander. The professional organ can propose something, but the commander would need to decide what to do. Sometimes the commander personally needs to go to a unit where there are problems. We had a case where both the commander and the deputy commander were killed, so the unit was left without leadership. I personally had to go to deal with the situation, appoint new commanders, stabilize the situation, and so on and so forth. This is very complicated. It's a very subtle operation that has to be executed in a very professional manner in the shortest period of time as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, in the answer you just gave us, you talked about what can be done at the brigade level, sometimes they need your help, from your corps level professional organ, then you said: "There are things that can done at the level of the corps ..." And then you said: "In our assessment there are also things that the main..." and then you said: "The Supreme Command should do" which are essential to be dealt with. I just want to talk about the other level that's in there between the corps and the Supreme Command and that's the Main Staff. So can you give us some idea of what the Main Staff morale organ would be doing in this process?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, an assessment would also be made on the basis of these elements, look at the positive and negative aspects and propose to the commander certain measures from their professional domain that they felt would need to be done in order to improve the situation in places where the situation was not so good. So they would have the same responsibility that we have at the corps level, except they are responsible for the entire army. Their procedure or method of work is similar, but the concept of their security guards is a little bit different than in my case. I had a smaller group of people, but they had more reports.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, the interpreters didn't catch your last sentence, if you could repeat it, please. What we have is: "Their procedural method of work is similar, but the concept of their security guards is a little bit different than in my case. I had a smaller group of peoples, but they had more reports." Then you said something else which the interpreters didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I thought that I had -- I improved but again I am making same mistake, Your Honours. I apologise. The method of assessment is the same as in the corps, but the morale organ at the Main Staff is not conceived in the same way as the morale organ in the corps. The corps, other than the morale duties, my men there, like I said, also were overseeing the situation in Batkovic. They had information activities, they had a press centre that was publishing a paper called, "Cooperation with international organisations and exchange of prisoners of war," which was not the case in other corps or at the Main Staff. It was not something that they will dealt with, the morale organ, so I would like this to be taken into account there. A higher command at the strategic level, so they are organised in a different way. I can speak on the basis of my own experience. Your Honours, I did not attend any analysis that were carried out at the level of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, carrying on with your answer to Mr. Grady's question, when you were talking about the monthly morale reports that your corps sent to the Main Staff. You said: "And then the last is our request for our superior bodies. So the Main Staff and the state leadership to do -- to carry out. So when Gvero receives these reports from the visual corps, he then compiles them into a document and then he would compile a report about the situation of combat morale of the army which is then first sent to Mladic and then the Supreme Command, Karadzic. And based on the problems seen in the reports and the requests submitted in the last item, we would usually receive a document from the Main Staff regulating our request, regulating the issue which would usually say ..." And now you're quoting in your answer. In your report, this number, you indicated that you had these problems: "We hereby inform you that since this problem is not in our jurisdiction, we have introduced, we have made the Supreme Command aware of it and expect to receive whatever you were requesting, additional men or something, expect to be to receive them within ten days or something like that." So, in your experience, General, is that how it worked, the request from the corps would go to the Main Staff up to President Karadzic and then back down to you in terms of trying to solve whatever the morale problems or issues that you were bringing to the attention was your superior command?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours, but we still need to differentiate one thing. There were things that the Main Staff could deal with and to assist us with, and they would immediately respond; but what was not in their jurisdiction then he would they would send that as a request upwards. They would not refer to the Supreme Command if they could deal with something themselves, I am speaking about these matters in principle. And I did note certain problems there, especially in respect of the cadre -- the morale cadre when I had to replace my assistant and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you told the OTP during your 2004 interview that General Gvero often called you, and I know it's going back a ways; but can you give the Trial Chamber an example, say, any time in 1995 of what you're talking about when you're dealing with General Gvero regarding morale problem or issue in your corps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, General Gvero was one of our most senior generals and he was very much respected. He was extremely professional, and he never called my morale organs and bypassed me. If he had my requests for them, he would first call me and then say, Commander, Jelacic did not send such-and-such report to me. We asked for this. We still have not received it. Could you please see what is going on there with that. Most often he would call when some deadline was looming that had to do with some sort of consultation. Often they would call me to attend consultations where the municipal -- or the Mayor's would assemble and where the Supreme Command members were present or the prime minister and these matters or meetings had to do with conducting the war and he would say it would be good for you also as the commander to attend or the commander ordered for you to report there at such and such a time and can you send me a report about what happened there. These were these situations. Otherwise, when he was passing through my area of responsibility he would always stop at my command post, even if it was for ten minutes. He was a very professional officer, and I would always learn something from talking with him. He would never issue orders, though. I would just like to say once more, Your Honours, the nature of his duties and considering the kind of person he was, he was not a man who tended to issue orders. I think in the army only his first posting was a command post, all the other posts he held were morale posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to show you a document in the ten minutes we have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's 5D974.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We looked at this last Thursday. It's your attack order from the Spreca operation, and I just want to ask you a couple of questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 5 of the English, and this will also be page -- excuse me, 5 of the B/C/S, please. And I think it's pretty much towards the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see where it says: "Military police units shall focus on providing security to persons in the command post ..."

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that. Could we scroll --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We need to scroll up --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- up please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- please. Other way. We need to go to the top of the document, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see the reference to the military police at the very top of the document, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it -- it states that the military police will be responsible for security of the prisoners of war, and then the next paragraph we see it says: "After brief interviews, the prisoners of war are to be escorted to the Batkovic collection centre for further treatment and processing. Prevent any abuse of the prisoners of war with a view to their possible exchange for our captured soldiers." With respect to these types of operations in your corps, was this standard procedure, General, that the military police would be responsible for POWs and that after a brief interview the POWs would be escorted to a location here, the Batkovic collection centre?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a prisoner of war is first brought in by the brigade police to a certain location where the intelligence officers try to find out interesting information from them in order to understand the situation among the enemy, the number of troops, equipment, which is regular procedure; and then they inform the corps command that they have captured a prisoner of war. The security organ of the corps immediately sends a military police patrol, with a vehicle, and takes the prisoner of war after the interview and takes him directly to the Batkovic collection centre. And the camp commander immediately informs the International Committee of the Red Cross who also come then to take his particulars. When they are taking the person's particulars, this is usually done in the presence of a representative of the ICRC. And once he provides his particulars, he's protected, he has certain rights to contact his family and so on and so forth. In all the unfortunate circumstances that he finds himself in, he is allowed some certain measures that would make his life easier. We had extremely good cooperation with the 2nd corps of the B and H army; and we would quickly exchange these people for our fighters who are captured on the other side or for our men who happened to be in prison; for example, in Tuzla, who were detained for some political reasons. That was how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your 2004 OTP interview, General, you stated pretty concisely, and let me just quote you: "Once somebody surrenders, they are no longer a threat. All you can do with them is feed them, dress their wounds if they are wounded, and send them to a collection centre." Do you remember saying that in 2004?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Once they surrender, they no longer pose a danger to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when somebody is unarmed and in your custody, General, doesn't it kind of just come down to that, down to what you just said and what you said in 2004, that that's how POWs should be treated?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, once he finds himself to be in such a situation, to be captured, this unfortunate man is frustrated, frightened, afraid for his life. He's sorry -- a person in a sorry state, and the only thing that needs to be done for that person is to provide protection. You have to take them out of the combat action area. You don't want them to be exposed to fire, and that is how one should treat that person. I told all my commanders that a prisoner of war is also a Serb taken out of the POW camp from another side. So keeping an enemy soldier alive means also keeping our own soldier alive, and throughout the war, we were very careful to act in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see we are about a minute away from the break. This might be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer. How much longer do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I reduced the -- my outline by several sections over the break. I think I will still need the rest of my estimated time, though. So I think I am at about two and a quarter right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning again to you, General. We were looking at your Spreca 95 combat order.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's 5D974.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I see that it's still on your screen where it should be. If we look at item 7.6. Can we see that? Did we scroll down a little bit. Thank you. Do you see under the heading of "moral and psychological preparations" you order that: "Immediately before the commencement of the operations, inform all members of participating commands and units about the objective, importance, and tasks of the operation with particular focus on the following ..." And you have five bullet points of a military political nature listed there. Where would you obtain this information and analysis that you have contained here in your combat report -- combat order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in my previous answers I emphasize the fact that this operation started earlier than planned because it was supposed to be planned if the truce was violated; and our opponents violated the truce a lot earlier than we had expected, in fact. And this, in fact, was caused by the problems that we had on Majevica where the enemy tried to take the dominant elevations which included the Stolice relay. This position would have given the opponent very favourable conditions. Those are the highest elevations. After those elevations, the terrain is a lot lower, so the opponent would have had far more favourable conditions to continue with his combat operations. If those features in Semberija fell into enemy hands, then the territory of Republika Srpska would have been divided into two parts, and that would have meant that this territory couldn't be integral. There would be problems when it comes to logistic, et cetera, and command. As for the measures that have to be taken with regard to moral and psychological preparations, well, these are measures that are the result of experience and they are based on the assessment of morale for the previous year. And it also concerns measures that have to be taken, usual measures that have to be taken when you engage in combat operations. This was all decided on -- on the basis of consultations with my associates, the Chief of Staff and other assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, first bullet point refers to the international situation and refers to current activities of the contact group members and specifies Russia, where you would you, General, obtain, this type of information? I take with all your other duties you didn't have time to read all of the international political journals and so forth. How were you kept abreast of these types of political international developments?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First part was information we'd get from the Main Staff, usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who at the Main Staff would give you that information?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information would arrive by post. The documents drafted by the body that dealt with such subjects, such issues, and General Gvero was responsible for this body.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in your experience, General, why is it important to include this type was information in a combat order?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were involved in a particular kind of war. In territory where our enemy used to be our friend, apart from defensive purposes, the war also had the characteristics of a civil war and to a certain extent the characteristics of a religious war, but it was a local war for sure. The enemy spoke the same language, they used the same weapons, they had finished the same military academies, which rendered the entire situation more complicated when it came to preparing for combat operations and when it came to organising ourselves. The first item is a result of the of the fact that we didn't have time to follow the situation on the political scene. It was so that the soldiers could understand the circumstances within which we were acting. Preparations had already been -- were already underway to finish the war. It was necessary to preserve the territory as it was at the time. It was necessary to create favourable conditions for our negotiators so that they could put an end to the war without encountering any significant problems or without having to make any significant concessions which would be to the detriment to the people. They had to take disciplinary measures to contribute to such an outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, picking up on what you told us on Friday with the level of morale being in -- in your own words second in importance only to the training, is it fair to say that when you say that people -- the fighters had to understand what it was that they were fighting for, that that is an essential element of combat readiness. That is that your soldier in the trench understands what it is that he is putting his life on the line for and that he agrees with the goals of the struggle?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. However, I have to correct something here. The first factor has to do with the control and command. That's first item. First you have the commander, then you have morale, then you have training, and readiness. Your Honours, I have to quote. The Chinese military theoretician who said that a line in front of a horde of donkeys is more important than vice versa. So the commander's role is of key importance. Readiness for combat is also necessary, that is correct, but if you are willing to fight -- but if you don't -- if on is really prepared to sacrifice one's self for the war's objectives, then other problems will not be that important. The task will be carried out regardless of extremely difficult circumstances, but I won't address the matter of other factors. But yes, this is very important. It's also important that -- to say that the organ for morale doesn't act in this manner. Morale is affected by the Supreme Command, by the local community, by how one's family has been taken care of. Well, the kind of food one receives also affects one's morale. Unfortunately, we are only human and all these factors have an influence on morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, is it not the purpose of the morale organ from the lowest level all the way to the Main Staff constantly to assess those various factors that can affect morale to make sure that that fighting spirit is kept at the maximum level?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, and this is a suggestion made to the commander. The commander should take into consideration everything that is positive. He should support such positive factors and issue orders to that effect. In that spirit, if a commander doesn't adopt such factors, well, he's risking the possibility of having results that aren't that good or aren't as good as he expected. Then it can't be an error made by the organ of morale. If certain measures weren't accepted, measures that were put forward, well, then, one has to accept the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General, let's look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 5D982, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, we have a -- another document relevant to the Spreca 95 operation. It's an analysis after about a month of the operation being underway that was conducted. Take a moment and familiarise yourself with this document, General. I don't know if you've seen it recently.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the other part of the document, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may scroll down please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, I might be able to save us little bit of time, but do you remember -- and I don't want to go into all the details I think we've spoken about some of them generally already in answer to some questions, I think, from some of my learned friends. But, is it fair to say that for various reasons the Main Staff took other command of this operation, and as a result of the analysis that's set forth in this document certain conclusions were made in order, successfully, to complete the operation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I wasn't present. A representative of mine was. But yes, that would be the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, the abbreviation that we have in the original copy of this is NONO. It's been translated one way, but can you just tell us who that is, NONO; what that position is? It's identified as Colonel Gengo. And again, in 1995, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Colonel Gengo, you might find his name a little difficult to pronounce. He was the deputy of Chief of Staff of operative and training; and here the abbreviation used was from the operations and training organ. So he is a professional involved in documents on combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now if we could look at item 3, and this is on page 4 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, but it's item number 3. Again, page 4 of the English page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It says that one of the general tasks to improve the operation is in addition to the officers from the VRS Main Staff, include one operations officer from each corps in the Main Staff IKM as well as an assistant commander for morale guidance and psychological propaganda. Do you see that, General? Number 3.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So my question to you is, General, do you recall why it was important to have that assistant commander for morale actually located in the Main Staff IKM?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is some misleading question on my learned friend, because this is assistant commander, the corps assistant commander, not the -- for morale. Not "Main Staff." It says, "Assistant commander for the Main Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a comment, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I identify any organ or any level of command in my question, so I think my friend is again making speaking objections. I simply asked why was it important to have an assistant commander for morale guidance and psychological propaganda in the Main Staff IKM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a perfectly legitimate question which the witness can answer, I am sure. General, could you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know why the Chief of Staff from the Main Staff decided to adopt this conclusion, whether there was a problem when it came to information or motivating these units or something else. I don't know. I cannot claim for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at page 6 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. We're looking at item 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It says: "By means of extra effort on the part of all subjects, especially the command and control and organs in charge of morale, we have to explain to the soldiers the goals, current results, and final consequences of a successful completion of this operation thereby reestablishing the level of morale from the beginning of the operation and creating conditions for an even greater pace in conducting tasks from Operation Spreca 95." General, does that jog your memory at all as to why it was important for General Milovanovic to place a morale assistant commander in the Main Staff IKM for the remainder of this operation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can't see what you have just read out. Could you show it to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's on -- it's number 8, General. And we can blow that up if that helps?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it now, Your Honours. Your Honours, I will have to explain the situation to you again, the situation that prevailed. When the Spreca Operation commenced, we regained lost territory on Majevica; however, the imminent end of war, and we were all aware of this imminent end - that included the soldiers - and publically expressed idea that the Republika Srpska would accept the ratio of 51:49 and the fact that the weather was very bad, there was snow, a lot of snow; all these factors had a negative influence on soldiers' morale and their desire to continue with combat. Soldiers would say, Well, if you want to have this hill, we have more than about 30 per cent of territory than what we are supposed to have according to the peace agreement. If you want this hill, exchange it for some other hill or for two other hills. So, in a certain sense, we tried to motivate them, but we weren't successful in doing this. I was aware of the fact, especially, because in accordance with an order from the Main Staff I had to send some of the forces to other corps; and I didn't have sufficient men to engage in maneuvers in that operation in tasks and to have reserve forces for the corridor, which is where I was expecting a large-scale attack to be launch, and I wanted to prevent this from happening. So I personally was not convinced that this operation would be successfully brought to an end. All the attempts we made, the attempts to raise morale and so on and so forth, bore no fruit. You know when soldiers adopt a certain position, which was in fact correct, you know, we can chew over the fat here now, but the facts are such. They weren't prepared to sacrifice themselves towards the end of the war. They weren't prepared to sacrifice themselves for -- to engage in attacks, but they were prepared to defend the positions that we were already located at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, tell us what some of those attempts were, General, to raise the morale in line with this analysis here in this document.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, going to low level commands, speaking to the troops, trying to persuade them, unfortunately a state of war hadn't been declared. Legal elements more present. The possibility of sanctions wasn't a possibility; such a possibility has a good effect when it comes to carrying out one task -- one's task. When there are no military laws or war laws, all one could do was try to persuade soldiers, explain things to them. This does not always bear fruit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the next paragraph, paragraph number 9, General, it states: "We believe that once the VRS Main Staff takes over the command of the operation, the faith of all participants that this operation is of great importance and that the further course of VRS operations this year, or even in this war, depends on it." Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, given the importance of these military developments and your response to it, the importance of the Spreca 95 operation, given the difficulties that you just told us about, raising combat morale of the troops in connection with this important operation, with so much at stake, General Gvero was certainly kept informed of these developments, wouldn't you say?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the course of the operation everyone was informed, that included corps that weren't involved in the operation. They were informed through reports from the Main Staff. We sent out part of the report to the Main Staff, but there was a lack of knowledge; so there was a central report that informed us of what was happening at other fronts. So in addition to information on morale, well, General Gvero and everyone else in the Main Staff were in a position to follow the course of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I'm not speaking about General Gvero being privy to information as somebody that's simply being sent a copy of the report. My question to you is given the import of this operation, the problems that you had raising morale, isn't it the fact -- isn't it the case that General Gvero was informed about these problems that you were having raising combat morale naturally through either his professional line or through somebody in the command structure at the corps level, such as yourself?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. Naturally he was informed of this, and he was the one who would follow and assess morale in the ranks of the entire army. So naturally he was informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General, I'd like to move to another topic. There --

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the fifth topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we have a few more to go, General, so have a drink of water and I'll have one with you.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Cheers.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in Bijeljina there was an investigation prison. I believe its name was Zitopromet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you have a military or civilian prison in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, when I use the term "investigation prison," does that mean anything in particular to you? Does that term connote anything to you as opposed to the Batkovic prison, for example?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batkovic was a camp for POWs. It wasn't a prison. I'm sorry. There is a barracks prison, and there are prisons where you serve your sentence for having committed a crime. Such a prison, criminal prison was in Zitopromet, near the train station; but it was the responsibility of the Ministry of the Interior. It was not the responsibility of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, do you recall the Red Cross inquiring about the fate of a Muslim man from Zepa sometime about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, well, first of all, I received a request from Ms. Renn [phoen], who was an associate of the general secretary of the UN for human rights or humanitarian affairs. I can't remember the exact name of the body. She asked me to help her clear up the case of Mr. Avdo Palic, a Colonel. He was the commander for the defence of Zepa, as far as I understood. According to what Mr. Palic's wife said the last time he was seen was in a prisoner called Vanikov Mlin in Bijeljina barracks. That's where. There was a barracks prison and there was a part of the prison where those suspected of having committed crimes were interrogated regardless of their ethnic origin or of the army they belonged to. I immediately took certain measures. I was provided with an original document in which one could see that the gentleman left the prison alive and good health, and he was handed over to Captain Pecanac from the Main Staff. He came in a Golf vehicle, a red Gold. I can't remember the number plate, and he set off in the direction of the Main Staff. I told the lady that I had no other information on what happened to him afterwards. I told the same thing to your colleagues when I had an interview with the Prosecution with regard to this case. I didn't know you would ask me about this. Had I known, I could have brought those documents that demonstrate that we acted in accordance with the law and that he left these premises alive and in good health, but as to what happened to him later on, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when Colonel Palic left that prison. And again, I'm sorry, General, could you say the name of the prison slowly for the record, because I don't think we got it, this prison where he was being detained.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the prison was called Vanikov Mlin or Vanex [phoen] Mill, and I really don't remember the date because I didn't prepare for all these questions. The Prosecutor is guiding me through the whole war and I'm an elderly man, and I can't remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you give us a year General, please.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know the year. It's 1995. 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, it was Eastern Bosnia Corps military policemen who guarded that facility where Mr. Palic was detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honours. But, monitoring this the facility was within the responsibility of the Main Staff. The garrison's prison was within the responsibility of my chief of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who at the Main Staff had responsibility over that prison, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ. And who specifically, I don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you mentioned a -- Mr. Pecanac, had you ever dealt with that individual before in your role as corps commander?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't have any contact with him when he took away Palic either. He did so with our professional persons. He is a younger officer. I don't exactly know even what position he held in the Main Staff, so I didn't have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: New topic, General. Last Friday you were asked by my learned friend from the Gvero Defence some questions about why General Gvero was at the Drina Corps IKM at Pribicevac on 9 July 1995. You remember those questions, right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember, Your Honour. I don't know why he was there. I learned later -- I heard that he was there in passing. The road was blocked, and he stopped by at the command post. My statement to your colleagues in this connection can be reduced to a hypothesis because I didn't know whether the Main Staff post was formed nor whether General Gvero was part of it nor why he was there. Now, if the command ordered him to be there at the forward command post and to carry out certain tasks relative to information and morale, he would be there. I really don't know whether he was there, know for how long he was there, so what I don't know, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, what I do want to ask you, General, is again you repeated today that you learned later -- and on Friday you said that you learned some years later, that General Gvero had just chanced to pass by Pribicevac. When did you actually learn this and how did you learn this, from whom did you hear this account?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
