utterances.text: Your Honours, throughout the war I was the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps; and I followed the trial of my colleague, General Krstic, with attention and from various answers and statements there I could gain a picture as to who moved through the command of the Drina Corps and who was where at what time. So that is what I base my knowledge on. I have no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can and did you ever tell my friends from the Gvero Defence team that it was just your supposition based on just follow the Krstic trial that that's how you came to the conclusion that General Gvero just chanced to pass through? Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can confirm what I know, what I personally witnessed, and things I can check out from several sources. My statements here are simply hypothetical suppositions. I can't say for how long, at what time, where people were at what time; so please I would appeal to you not to ask me questions that I cannot answer. I am under oath, and I have to tell the truth here.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, my last question then, General, is when you were answering the question to my friend from the Gvero team about what General Gvero was doing at Pribicevac, that was just a hypothetical supposition when you answered his question, right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honours, because I really do not have knowledge as to what specifically General Gvero was doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified last Thursday that you only learned about the Srebrenica operation by hearing the intensive artillery fire and then watching television.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to repeat what I have already said. I was surprised, and to tell you quite frankly, to a certain extent insulted because this was in my neighbourhood; and I wasn't informed of what was going on. I got the impression that I was not suitable and acceptable as someone who should know that this operation was being conducted. Earlier on we would always be informed, and I could assist by certain measures, actions, and so on. But in this case, I was bypassed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, General, to your best recollection as to the date of this trip to Pilica by your MPs is sometime after the fall of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the passage of time I can say that it was about the middle of the month of July; but I cannot tell you the exact date, perhaps if I were to see the document about the surrender of those prisoners, that would jog my memory. But speaking off the bat, it took time, logically, for them to get there, because the combat operations were not conducted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, General, I'll be able to help you out with that document, and we'll get to it, and then we'll be done today. Okay. My learned friend from the Pandurevic team showed you an entry in the Zvornik Brigade duty operations officer's notebook, which indicated that 35 soldiers from the East Bosnian Corps were sent to the IKM. And you don't need to repeat your testimony from last Friday on that, but you also testified that the POWs that Captain Vulin picked up were taken to Batkovic and exchanged a few days later for your men at Lisaca. Is that -- do I have that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the questions of Defence counsel was probably a confusion between the police and the military police, because even when the civilian police were there, they would say they were coming from Bijeljina, from my zone, from the East Bosnian Corps, because I didn't send a platoon there. I sent a company there headed by the commander of the company, and to make it serious, I also sent the battalion commander with a group of officers, Major Vulin, with that assignment. Secondly, they carried out that assignment within a period of four to five hours and returned back. So I don't even know where the forward command post was, but obviously it wasn't in Pilica judging by this. And my final answer to your question is that they were exchanged for soldiers captured at Lisaca, and not Vlasic. It was one of the peaks at Majevica where they were surrounded, and they couldn't break out; and through the mediation of the Red Cross, they surrendered and they were exchanged. I needed a certain number of prisoners of war because I didn't have a sufficient number for the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, your recollection is that that exchange occurred very soon after those prisoners were taken to Batkovic, a matter of days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you with precision, but I think it was soon. We needed the men and that is why we intervened. I know that Major Vulin went there once again, and I think that he brought back wounded prisoners of war from the hospital in Bratunac who were also brought to the prisoner of war camp in Batkovic and who were also exchanged, I think there were about 30 of them, one bus load of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, other than Major Vulin, from whom did you receive any reports or have any discussions for that matter about this trip with the trucks to pick up the approximately 100 prisoners in the middle of July?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I spoke also to my chief of security, because he had professional monitoring over the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified that the prisoners were being held in an elementary school in Pilica. Did Major Vulin tell you how they got there, how they knew where it was located, how they found this location?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in Pilica there was a police checkpoint which stopped the column; and when he said who he was and why he was there, he said that the school was in the immediate vicinity, and the prisoners of war were there. I was informed by him that he emptied out the gym in that school and that all the people who were held in that gym, were put on the vehicles and driven away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, as you sit here, you're certain that it was the school in Pilica and not the cultural centre, the Dom?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really can't say with certain, but from a facility that was in the immediate vicinity of the road, I gathered it was the school but it may I have been the cultural centre also. This may be important for the Prosecution, for me as the commander it wasn't so significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, in your 2007 interview with the OTP, General, you related to the investigators something you were told. And I just want to quote your answer, this is at page 90. You said: "I heard from one of my commanders that they actually collected people from one school, and these guards were getting ready to kill them all. He told me that when he issued an order for them to enter the trucks, that they were not using the steps. They were jumping in. They were so happy to be imprisoned." Do you recall telling the investigators that in 2007, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't remember that I said that they were getting ready to kill them, because I didn't know that; but it is true that Major Vulin told me that they were running and jumping into the vehicles, they even got stuck at the gates of the building. They were hurrying to leave because they were told they were going to be exchanged, and they were happy to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, General, as you sit here today you deny telling the prosecution and the investigators in 2007 that one of your commanders told you that when they got to the school, that the guards there were ready to -- or getting ready to kill them all, you deny saying that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the passage of time, I can't be sure whether I said that or not. It is not my intention to mislead anyone, but most often I don't say what -- things I don't really know. Maybe I did say that. I'm not sure. I still have the tapes from that interview, and I'll listen to them again to check; but I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, General, that's a pretty significant thing to be told and to not be sure about whether you then told us about that. I mean, you were get a report from one of your subordinates that they interrupted a mass execution. How can you not be sure that you received that information? It sounds ...

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, for executions and the things that happened, people heard about this much, much later because it was covered with a kind of veil of secrecy. And during my service, I heard all kinds of things, but I also checked out all kinds of things; and I'm telling you quite frankly and sincerely that in view of the time I cannot claim with certainty whether I actual said that or not. I don't have the transcript in the Serbian language of my statement, but I do have all the tapes, and I really will listen to them all again when I get home. I certainly have no intention of pre-empting anything. I am glad, if we did prevent an execution, which we probably did, because the investigators told me that these were among the few that were exchanged. But I do not wish to enter into polemics with you on this issue. I agree that it has its weight. I am a serious person, and I have no intention of denying something I said. If I had said that, it would have probably stuck in my memory. Everything is possible though, Your Honours, I mean one mustn't forget the time factor. These things should have been discussed three or four years ago or three or four years after the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me show a photograph, General, and I'm going to move on to a new area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's 65 ter page -- sorry, 1936, and we'll be looking at page 36 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, do you have a paragraph buffer on your screen?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The soldier on the right with the number 2 marking him, do you recognise that individual?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: His name is Radenko Tomic, and he was at the time a member of the Panteri unit subordinated to your corps. His nickname is Gargijia; and this photograph was taken of him in Potocari on the 12th of July. It's actually part of a video showing him and other soldiers entering Potocari. General, as commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, did you ever become aware that the Panteri unit was present in Potocari on 12 July?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were cases of large changes in the Panther's unit, there was a constant fluctuation of personnel there of soldiers coming and going. The name of this soldier doesn't mean anything to me, and I don't know whether he was a member of the brigade or had left the brigade and joined one of the other units. There were cases of soldiers leaving a unit and going to another part of the front where combat operations were ongoing. There were people who wanted to be constantly on the go, to be active. The Bijeljina Light Infantry Brigade did not participate, but whether certain individuals may have participated without the knowledge of their superiors, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you, General, that Mr. Tomic identified himself in that photograph and has told us that he was an active member of the Panteri unit at that time. Does that change your recollection at all?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. I can't -- I don't have the tone. It's possible that he was. It's possible that he was a deserter, but that he was under the command of the brigade. When he was in Potocari, he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you 65 ter 330, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if you would, General, just have a look at this. I don't know if you've ever seen it before, probably not, so take your time. And I want to particularly direct your attention to paragraph 2 of this interim combat report by Commander Pandurevic on 16 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see this document for the first time, and this is the first time that somebody from the military police of the Eastern Bosnian Corps took part in the combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, General, my question to you is you've been very clear in your testimony thus far that no elements from the Eastern Bosnia Corps participate in the Srebrenica operation. Having seen this interim combat report are you changing your testimony about that, or do you dispute what this interim combat report clearly states; that is, that a part of your military police platoon was involved in the cleansing operation, sealing off, and searching the terrain?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I state that according to what I know, no unit or part of the unit participated in this operation. This is news to me. I really don't know if it's true or not true, but this is the first time that I'm seeing a document like this. As far as I know, no one went there or took part.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General, this Trial Chamber has heard the testimony of Drazen Erdemovic, a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who belonged to the Bijeljina platoon of the detachment. And he has testified that on 10 July he was in the Bijeljina barracks and was ordered to Srebrenica, which he entered with his unit on the 11th was July. And you testified that you followed the Krstic trial, surely you know about Mr. Erdemovic's guilty plea and his testimony; right, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Erdemovic was a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment which was under the command of the Main Staff. It was not under the command of the East Bosnian Corps. He could have happened to be in the barracks after the activities in Majevica when they came as reinforcements but that does not mean that he was under my command or that he had gone there under my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, General, there is no suggestion from me that that was the case. My question to you is you must be familiar with his testimony that on the 16th of July, the same date that Commander Pandurevic's interim combat report indicates that your military police platoon is in his area of responsibility, that members of that 10th Sabotage Detachment participated in a mass execution at the Branjevo farm, and that later that day went over to the Pilica cultural centre and participated in another mass execution there before returning to his barracks in Bijeljina. Were you aware of that, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, there is also testimony from two survivors who testified from the 14th to the 16th of July, 1995, they were detained at the Pilica school where prisoners were also shot. Did you ever hear that information, General, following the Krstic trial or any time since July of 1995 when these events occurred?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't hear it in 1995. I heard about it when the trial was going on, actually, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you heard about these executions occurring in the Pilica area, particularly in the school, where you've told us your military policemen, in your words, probably saved people from a mass execution, did you ever put that testimony and your recollection of those events together in that members of your unit were present when this mass execution occurred on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to information I received from the battalion commander, they didn't stay longer. They returned immediately. And I had no information that they were present then or took part in the event. Judging by how quickly they came back, I assumed that they returned immediately, as soon as they took the people, they came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, General, since we are touching this area, here, and a few days have passed since you started your testimony here, I would like to remind you of the advisory I gave you in the beginning of your testimony in relation to your rights under our rules, rights against self-incrimination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, General Simic's answer, which appears in line 9 on page 55, is not clear to me. The General answered that he didn't know, but what he didn't know, is what? Whether the massacre at Pilica Dom in Branjevo took place, or whether his platoon went there or not? So if you could clear that up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A very valid point. Could you -- thank you, Judge Kwon --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you take this up with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, did you understand His Honour's question. You testified that you didn't find out in 1995. You found out sometime later, following the Krstic trial, so the question is what did you find out later, that there were executions in Pilica, that your MPs were there during that period of time, or what exactly did you find out later? Can you clarify that, please for the Trial Chamber, whether --

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thought that I was clear. I found out about the execution much later when I found out the trial of General Krstic was underway. I had never heard yet that my unit or any part of it had participated in the operation itself or in the executions. What I know is that we had picked up the prisoners and that I was told that there was still some left at the facility in Pilica, that they had just emptied the sports hall at the school. Only later did I find out that there were some executions also at Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it to you whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you leaving this topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I have a few more questions on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- this topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, did you ever talk to General Miletic again after all this information that you learned from the Krstic trial? Did you ever talk to General Miletic given this conversation that you had with him sometime in mid-July that you've been telling us about when he said -- or when he was listening in on the conversation and General Krstic said there were no prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I live in Banja Luka in Republika Srpska, and General Miletic lives in Belgrade. After the war, we never met, and we were not able to speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, did you ever make any effort to determine where those executions occurred, either before the Krstic trial or certainly after the Krstic trial, seeing as how it involved your neighbour and that your forces, very likely, given your own recollection of the time-frame, were present during these executions in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't know that any -- or I don't know that any of my forces were present during the executions. To this day, I doubt if any of my units participated in that operation. I state with full authority that this did not happen, that I was aware of or that the corps commander was aware of. So I do not want to have words put in my mouth. I heard about it during the trial of General Krstic. I did have the opportunity to talk with him about it at some training, but this was not something that I had heard about. I had found out about it from the media, I asked him, Is this really what happened? And he told me that this is enemy or hostile propaganda. Your Honour, my position is that no -- that a single prisoner that is killed that constitutes a terrible crime, and I cannot justify any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, again, General, my question is much simpler than that. You've told this Trial Chamber about a conversation you had with General Miletic in mid-July of 1995 that led to your forces picking up prisoners in Pilica. You subsequently received information about executions in Pilica. My question is: Did you ever make any effort to determine whether or not your troops had any involvement in those executions? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I learned about it, I was no longer working. I had been retired for quite some time. I did meet with the MP battalion commander, the then-Major Vulin, who is now a colonel; and I asked him again if our units had any part in that, because he was also put on some list as being one of the participants in the Srebrenica operation. Your Honours, he assured me and swore to me that they had nothing to do with the executions at Pilica. Your Honours, I have my area of responsibility that is under my care, and it's not up to me to investigate what others did. This is always something that is part of the duties of my superior or the prosecuting organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you met with Major Vulin again and asked him if your units had taken any part in those executions, is that when he told you, General, that when they arrived there the guards were about to kill those prisoners before they took them away? Is that when he told you that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that at that time. Please, again I am saying that I do not recall saying that in my statement, but the security -- and there was a lot of the security staff and a lot of soldiers around the school. He told me that and they ran willingly out of that gym, and they willingly entered the transport vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I want to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: P334, 00334. It's an interim combat report again by Commander Pandurevic. This one dated the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It will be up on your screen shortly. If you look at paragraph 2, General, there is a reference, again, to two platoons of the Bijeljina military police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, Your Honours. Suddenly we have one platoon and then suddenly we have two platoons. I don't know if we are going to get up to a battalion. I don't know. This is completely new, as far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may I have P151, please. If we can look at paragraph 2 in both versions. This is a Drina Corps daily combat report to the Main Staff, same day on the 18th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just in case there was any ambiguity about the reference to the Bijeljina military police, this report specifically refers does it not, General, paragraph 2, to two Eastern Bosnia Corps military police platoons successfully repelling all enemy attacks from the front and carrying out the blockading and combing of the terrain in the Zvornik Brigade AOR. And General, let me, before I put my question to you, and I am going to save some time. There is another couple of documents I was going to show you, but the fighting during this period of time was particularly fierce and costly to Commander Pandurevic's units. It was some of the most deadly fighting of the war, and your units were there in that area of responsibility. Is it your testimony that as Eastern Bosnia Corps commander, you never became aware that military police platoons under your command were involved in this fierce fighting, these scouring of the terrain activities in mid-July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a report of the Drina Corps, and this paragraph is totally copied from the report of the Zvornik Brigade. As far as I am concerned this is a completely new document, and I didn't have the opportunity, as yet, to see this document. And for the 15th time I am saying, Your Honours, according to my information, no unit of the military police from the Eastern Bosnia Corps participated in the combat actions. I don't know of it. Once again, I say I have my own troubles. And I was in the corridor, and I don't know that this unit participated. Had I known that I would have probably had said that in my earlier interviews that I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, could I just interrupt you for a second. General, assuming the reports are correct, do you have any explanation of how the two military police platoons could have been present from your command without your knowledge? Do you have any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that period I had my units in several sections of the front to assist. I have a battalion, a Bijeljina brigade in the Sarajevo Romanija AOR. I had problems at Majevica, also in the corridor and so on and so forth. According to what I know, I did not order them to go there, and I don't know about this. Had I known of it -- I mean, I have no reason to hide anything, I would have stated that in my interviews previously with the OTP. I do not have information if any of my associates ordered and implemented that. I mean, I am saying now I will just have to make inquires about it. But, at this point, I truly say that I don't know that that unit participated in that. I was surprised when earlier at General Pandurevic's, he asked me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How will you investigate if necessary? Who will you ask about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am going to ask my deputy, General Gavric first, because he was at Majevica, and I was in Posavina. So he was in Bijeljina more often than I was, and this prompts me to go to the archives where the documents of my corps are archived. This is in the Bijeljina barracks, and I would like to go through all of these reports to see if I, perhaps, am mistaken. This is totally new, as far as I am concerned, because as a commander, I am ashamed in a way to be given certain information that I really was not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, you testified that your conversation with General Miletic, trying to locate some prisoners to exchange, whatever that actual day was, you testified that General Miletic didn't seem to have any knowledge of what was going on regarding the Srebrenica operation much less knowledge about prisoners of war. Although, he agreed to coordinate your MPs into that adjoining corps; is that correct? And let me just ask that again. I'm sorry, that was a terrible question. It's actually two questions. When you spoke with General Miletic on that occasion, he didn't seem to have any knowledge about what was going on with respect to the Srebrenica operation much less information about prisoners?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. That was the impression I got. Had he known that there were prisoners of war somewhere, he would have probably told me to go and pick them up and not to go and capture them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 192, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, take a moment and look at this document if you would. Have you seen this before? And don't answer until you've had a chance to look at it. I want to give you are an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I haven't seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, this communication from Colonel Savcic to General Mladic and General Gvero, refers to General Tolimir proposing several measures; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, but I cannot see the date here. All I can see is 14 hundred hours, but I can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can help you there, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If you scroll down a little bit in the original, and scroll over to the left just a little bit. There we are. You see July 13th at 1510 hours.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, this is probably the operator noting down when this was submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we scroll up to the top, General, it says: "That there are over a thousand members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba)," do you see that, "Under the control of the military police Battalion of the 65th.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we scroll down, or if you look at number 4, it states that: "Once the commander of the military police battalion receives this order, he shall contact General Miletic and receive from him additional orders and verify if the proposal has been approved by the commander of the Main Staff." Now, General, this document shows does it not that General Miletic, by the 13th, certainly knew about at least a thousand prisoners that the VRS had under its control, does it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, before you answer the question, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President, this document wasn't even addressed to General Miletic. We don't know whether he received this information. One doesn't know ever received this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm going to rephase -- I'm going to add more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's hear the rephrasing of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, given your experience, your extensive command operational experience, knowing how the communications worked throughout the VRS, this document bears no indication that there would have been any reason for the normal course of communications to have been interrupted for any reason, is there? You've got a set stamp, you've got all the addressees.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all I don't see the stamp. All I can see is that this was sent off or dispatched by telegram or however. From this document -- I mean you say that I am experienced, so we can see from this document that General Miletic is only mediating between that person and the commander, and that the commander will receive the document and will say to Miletic, When they call you tell them I approve it. He doesn't even have to know what it was. Whatever Savcic was requesting was approved. This is how I understand this. I cannot say here that he knew about it or that he received the whole integral document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's 12.30, Mr. Thayer, shall we have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President, and I am very close to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So we'll have a -- very close by how much?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: By about 15 minutes, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And there will be a redistrict, I am sure, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but I'll do my best to conclude by the end of the day. This will be possible, I think, if the Prosecution really doesn't take up more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll try to shorten it to 10 minutes. Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, if you could conclude in ten minutes it will be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I will do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, good afternoon again.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see P02082, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I am going to show you a document, and it's related, I believe, to something you mentioned earlier today in your testimony, and that is a second trip that your MPs took to the Zvornik Brigade AOR. I beg your pardon, the Drina Corps AOR. And that was with respect to some wounded who had been evacuated from the Bratunac hospital. I think you told us a little bit about that, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see we have the wrong document up on the screen. Bear with me one moment. Forgive me, I called up 2080, it's 2082.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So you can disregard the document that's currently on your screen, General. General, we can see that this is a list of persons to be transferred under guard, and it indicates that it is your 3rd Battalion of your military police who are doing that. And this is on the 18th of July. I don't think my friends will disagree that these 22 individuals were wounded persons who were being treated at the Bratunac hospital and were evacuated on the 17th. And do you recall, General, your military policemen escorting these individuals to Batkovic on the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do remember this because it was the Main Staff that issued an order to this effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall who at the Main Staff issued that order? Who or which organ?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we may have Exhibit 7D712.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I am going to show you a document that my friend from the Pandurevic Defence showed you on Friday. It's a document we've used before in this Court both by the Prosecution and the Defence. And this, as you'll see if we could go to the second page, is the list of prisoners who had been police in the Batkovic camp. And if we look at the second and third right-most -- forgive me, the -- if we go all the way to the right, there are two columns, one that says "dolazak" and one that says "odlazak." Do you see those columns?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the one on the left -- dolazak, basically means when they came in; and the second column, odlazak, basically means when they left the camp; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you can take my word for and if my friends disagree, I am sure they will correct me, but on that list that we just saw of the 22 wounded who were escorted by your MPs to Batkovic, we can find each one of their names on this list entering Batkovic on the 18th. And they are the first prisoners to arrive, according to this list, in July of 1995 and then we see prisoners, if you look at the dates, arriving on the 24th, 26th, and so forth of July. And that coincides with your recollection, General, does it not, that prisoners didn't start trickling into Batkovic until two or three weeks after the Srebrenica operation ended.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wasn't commander of the Batkovic camp. I also tried to get rid of that, but the Main Staff told me it should be in my area of responsibility. I wasn't happy with it being there. As to how they came and how they left, well, my commission followed that matter, but to be quite truthful I never entered the Batkovic camp. But if you allege that this is correct, it probably is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But, my question, actually, General, was more simple than that. Do you recall - throwing your memory back to this time-period - do you recall that prisoners didn't begin arriving at the Batkovic camp until some period of time after the Srebrenica operation had concluded; that is, they didn't start arriving until towards the end of July 1995? And if it -- if you can't remember, then you can't remember, that's fine and I'll move on. But that was the question I was asking.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember. This was not really a matter of interest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if we look at this list, there are no exchanges in July, and there are no exchanges in August; and if we look at this last column, the word "razmena" means "exchanged"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the people who were brought in to the camp were exchanged with the command of the 2nd Corps, and I think that the Prosecution has the relevant list. Major Vulin handed them over, but this is just a list. I don't know where those who are brought in from Pilica are listed, but they were certainly exchanged in a short period of time, that was intended. I don't know which list they are on, but I know there is a list according to which they were all handed over for an exchange. I was provided with that list and I have also noticed the Prosecution has the list. I was asked whether I knew these individuals, I don't know them, I cannot confirm their names, but I can confirm that my commander of the military police handed them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I wanted to press your memory, just a little bit about, General, is whether this exchange actually occurred very soon after these prisoners were brought to Batkovic or whether it was sometime after they were brought up. And just bear with me for a moment, if you would. Let me just explain a couple of things that you can take my word for, if you would. As I said, this list indicates that there are no exchanges in July, this are no exchanges in August, but there is an exchange in September; that is, September 12th. If you look just on this page right here, you will see a few entries for 12th September 1995 and then the word "razmena," exchanged. And I counted up all those exchanged names, and it totals 102 prisoners, which is pretty much what you told us was the number that your MPs picked up. Now, let me show you one final document, General, and I'll put my last question on this issue to you and tie this up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could see P3940. And if we could scroll up just a teeny bit so we can catch the -- a little bit higher. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, just take a look at this document, if you would. And unfortunately we do not have an English translation, so I will have to ask you some questions to make some sense of it. And whenever you are ready, General, if you could just tell the Trial Chamber what this letter is about.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document that I drafted in which I informed General Mladic that we have problems with the families of these captured soldiers. It's obvious that the exchange was late. Everything had been agreed, but the Main Staff objected to the exchange for reasons that are unknown to me. This has really refreshed my memory that the exchange wasn't carried out. I personally had problems, on a couple of occasions I received these families. We had people for an exchange but there was a problem when it came to communications between the commission for exchange and the Main Staff. I don't know why, but we had problems as a result. I don't know why, because everything had been prepared for this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General, so just to be clear, so having looked at this document is it your belief now that those hundred-or-so prisoners that your MP company went down to pick up, weren't exchanged until after this letter, certainly, as suggested by the list that we just looked at that showed 102 prisoners being exchange on September 12th.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. That's what these documents show. We were really willing to solve this issue, but the Main Staff objected to this exchange; and we couldn't carry it out without their agreement. The situation was complex, there was shelling, there were problems at the western front and so on. I really can't remember everything now, Your Honours. I'm quite tired, so I can't be precise, but I know that I personally had problems with these parents. On a number of occasions I had to calm them down, et cetera, in order to carry out the exchange as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, General, just one last set of questions for you. My friend from the Pandurevic Defence asked you on Friday what the date was of this conversation you say you had with General Miletic, and as you affirmed today when I followed up on that, you testified, and let me quote: "I thought it was before the fall of Srebrenica, but following the trial of General Krstic, I thought that these prisoners would not be able to arrive in the primary school in Pilica before the fall of Srebrenica. So this was after the fall of Srebrenica." Do you remember testifying to that on Friday, General?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so is it your testimony that following the Krstic trial was the key for you to figuring out the date of this conversation?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours, because I really didn't know that they had prisoners. I had prepared my unit to go and capture troops, and luckily, for me and for them, they were already down there; and that's how this was solved, otherwise they would have participated in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your memory of the date of this conversation was triggered while you were following the trial as it progressed. I don't know if you were following it on television or on the internet, but it was triggered at the time the trial was go on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. I'm not very good at memorizing dates, given the time that has passed, I can provide you with approximate dates; but if I can consult certain documents, I can refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, the Krstic trial ended in 2001, so my question for you is why did you say during both your 2004 and 2007 interviews two and five years after the Krstic trial ended, that the conversation with General Miletic occurred before the VRS had entered Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be frank, I didn't think that was important, because the discussion had to do with me and General Miletic was referred to. I really didn't pay any attention to -- to that. When preparing to come here, I went through my personal notes and the documents I had at my disposal. But there is no other secret reason for which I said this to the general. I didn't think that it was of any importance for me. I wasn't aware that this would be used in connection to General Miletic, but now I am a Defence witness, and I thought it was necessary for me to go into the matter in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Will you please try to conclude, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General, I thank you for your testimony. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I will really do my best to conclude today. With regard to the last question put to you by the Prosecution, do you remember what the position of Mr. Krstic was when you spoke to him when General Miletic put you in touch with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I first spoke to General Mladic, and he gave me the cold shoulder very rapidly. When the commander says, That's it, that's it. It's the end -- end of the discussion. I asked General Miletic to put me in touch with General Krstic. I didn't know that they were next to each other, standing next to each other. General Krstic was probably listening to my conversation with General Mladic because he practically repeated the very same words, and he also told me that they didn't have any prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know what position he held at the time that you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General Krstic, in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic was the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And now, I would like to ask you something about the proofing session that we had just prior to your testimony. Do you remember me putting your question as to whether your corps units were in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And could you tell me what your reply was to that question?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they did not participate in the action.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You had two interviews with the Prosecution in 2004 and 2007. Did OTP representatives ever suggest to you that your units participated in the combat in question?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, Your Honours. I was persuaded of the fact that they didn't, and I'm still persuaded of that fact to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: With regard to the prisoners that your corps officer, the officer for your military police, Dragisa Vulin, took -- or rather, escorted, do you remember what the OTP representative said about this in 2007? It's page 90 of the corrected version of the transcript was provided to us recently by the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the interview, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they said unfortunately these were the only prisoners who were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: General, I'll read out what we were provided with, and it appears that the OTP representative told you the following: [In English] "You saved all those people's lives." [Interpretation] Are those the words that you can, in fact, remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it was put differently. Unfortunately, they are the only members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were captured in this operation and were exchanged. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to move on to an entirely different subject. I would like to show the witness 6D311, document 6D311.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This is the response that you sent to General Subotic. My colleague suggested that it was a presentation that you had made when analysing the combat in January 1995. Can you tell us, very briefly, what elements constituted your presentation when you made this analysis?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, I have to say that these themes weren't part of Directive Number 7. These thesis, in fact, were supposed to be part of a special directive from the Supreme Command and this was to have to do with the problems that it appeared in the territory of all units; that included my corps. It had to do with the problems relating to continuing with combat activities. If you are asking me about this -- I don't know, are you asking me about the directive? I haven't fully understood your question. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't think I was very clear. Does this have anything to do with analysis of combat at the end of January, the analysis by the Main Staff of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this arrived when the analysis had been made, when we received the document in the units. This was an entirely new document that has nothing to do with the analysis of combat readiness. This is the analysis of the situation in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You said that afterwards you didn't receive any directives, but do you remember receiving an order from the president ordering you to take certain measures?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, we did receive an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at document 5D1397. This hasn't been translated, but we have an unofficial translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You see the date on this document? It is the 6th [as interpreted] of March, 1995, two days after you sent the response to General Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we show the text of this order, and look at it, and tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in the meantime for the record on line 25, page 75, it's not "6th of March," it should be "26th of March."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether this order has anything to do with the suggestion that you sent to General Subotic?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very little, very little.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you say that there is very little connection, you already told you us that the president did not accept your suggestions, but doesn't this order deal with the same subjects as your proposals?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we proposed concrete measures, and what was sent to us was in such general terms it was all in forces up to then, too; but it wasn't implemented. So I can say, in general terms, it was accepted but in concrete terms no order was given to carry it out, so I personally believe that my proposals were not adopted. Because I had proposed concrete measures, and this is a political document in which everything is described in very general terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to show you document 5D1322, page 33 in B/C/S and page 32 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before we get this document, it is the journal of the secretary of President Karadzic, but before you look at it, you remember that Directive Number 7 was dated the 8th of March 1995. And we've also seen that it was sent on the 17th of March 1995. If you look at the top of the page, you can see the date of the 15th March 1995. And then, we see the date 16th of May, but I think everyone agrees that, in fact, it should be the 16th of March 1995. One can verify this very easily. If you look at this date, the 16th of March 1995, and the entry for 1100 hours, you see, General Miletic [as interpreted], Tolimir, and Subotic.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to correct the transcript. On page 77, line 5, it's "General Milovanovic." Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: These persons, these generals, Milovanovic, Tolimir, and Subotic, were they qualified to have a discussion with the president regarding the directive?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know where they were there at all, please don't make me speculate. There is a Simic here, but that's not me, he's Drago Simic. You can see him mentioned here from 1605.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yes, we know that it's General Milovanovic. There is the abbreviation before his name.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, we can see that it's generals Milovanovic, Tolimir, and Subotic. They are all generals. But it doesn't say here what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And this meeting lasted from 1100 hours, 1105, until 1505 hours, that is what it says here -- 16. I'm sorry, I know that my next question is hypothetical, but you have answered a lot of hypothetical questions regarding the directive. According to your own experience, as a military man, as a general, do you have any idea what these generals may have discussed with General Karadzic on the eve of descending of Directive Number 7?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, probably about the conduct of the armed struggle. If a state of war had been normally declared, they would have become their advisors. I don't know whether he treated them now as his advisor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, Ms. Fauveau, we are in the sphere of pure speculation, so let's move to something more concretely, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You spoke of the assistant commanders of the Main Staff who moved two units. What were the best means of commander General Mladic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Milovanovic"] to know what the state of those units were?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic, page 78, line 11.

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You'll have to repeat the question now, because I got lost with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's try and speed it up, because it is obvious that the witness is very tired.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to finish very soon, I assure you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: What were the best means for General Mladic to get acquainted with the situation in his subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the best way is personal insight, to go on site and then no one can lie to you or mislead you or belittle the seriousness of the situation or anything else. So the best way is to go there personally and to see what's happening, and he did that very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could he, himself, personally go and visit all the units, always?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, he even exaggerated. He went personally to investigate the enemies. He had absolutely no fears in that respect. He over-did things. I was responsible for his security while he was in my zone of responsibility, but it was a great problem to secure his safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did he occasionally send his collaborators, his assistant?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, Your Honours, he would send his associates.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Judge Kwon, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Simic, one of the answers you gave to Mr. Thayer in the course of cross-examination drew my attention. In answering the events that happened in Srebrenica in the summer, you answered this way. It's page 51, line 11 to 14. You said, I quote: "Your Honours, for executions and the things that happened, people heard about this much, much later, because it was covered with a kind of veil of secrecy." And then you said: "And during my service, I heard all kinds of things, but I also checked out all kinds of things." What did you mean by that, that you checked out all kinds of things?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can link my answer to the question by Madam Fauveau. I get reports from the units, but I go and check them out, too. That is what I had in mind. As for these events, my possibilities were limited to check out those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that your testimony is that you didn't know, you were not aware of the operation that happened in Srebrenica. And you heard about those killings much, much later, but given your position and rank, would it be correct for me to assume that you may have some information with hindsight? Who did the killing and who did those reburial? Are you in the position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I saw most of the information and reports about these things in the foreign media. It appears to have been a taboo topic amongst us in Republika Srpska. At the level of the Main Staff, an analysis of the Srebrenica operation was never carried out so that we, from the other bodies, did not know at all how the operation was carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was your basis on your part when you recommended withdrawal to General Mladic when you learned that indictment had been issued?

utterances.speaker: NOVICA SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the indictment was issued, the president of the republic, who was also indicted, and General Mladic, were required to leave their positions because they had been indicted. In a military career, regardless of the kind of application, whether it's criminal or judicial proceeding, the person has to withdraw from his position until the proceedings are completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. That, General, brings us to the end of your testimony. You've been here quite a few days with us, and you've been very patient with us as well. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial as a Defence witness for General Miletic. And on behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, it was an honour for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't suppose we can finalise the documents in the remaining two or three minutes. Shall we leave them? Let's try, anyway. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I suspect my list is the shortest. To my surprise, I discover that P702 and P703 had not yet been admitted into evidence, so I will do so through this witness unless anybody's got any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would there be an objection, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I invite, with no objection to that application, could I invite the rest of these applications be put over to tomorrow. We would like to see and review --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- the lists of both the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough, fair enough. We accept the previous requests. Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So those two can be admitted, because I understand you, Mr. Josse, your reservation did not refer to those?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. So those two documents, Mr. Haynes, are being admitted. The rest we will deal with tomorrow when we reconvene in the afternoon at 2.15. By the way, in case you are not aware, we will be sitting in the afternoon tomorrow and Wednesday, but Thursday the sitting is in the morning and not in the afternoon. All right? Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning -- afternoon at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of November, 2008, at 2.15. p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
